metadata.title: Need-supportive teaching is positively associated with students' well-being: A cross-cultural study

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 secondary microdata for 15-year-old students across 70 economies, but the provided text does not report whether PISA sampling weights or replicate weights were applied in the HLM estimation. The authors describe a two-level HLM structure (students at level 1; schools at level 2) and include school SES and school composition covariates, which is consistent with accounting for clustering at the school level, but it is not the same as applying PISA complex-survey weights. Because no weight variable names (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or replicate procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife) are mentioned, the weighting approach cannot be confirmed from the manuscript excerpt. Analysts should, when reproducing, use the appropriate PISA student and school weights from the OECD database and apply replicate-weight variance estimation if available, to ensure population-representative inference under the complex sampling design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: plausible_values_handling is 'not_applicable' — the study likely does not analyze cognitive achievement PVs (e.g., it may focus on affective/attitudinal outcomes, curriculum data, or non-ILSA micro-data).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 student questionnaire data for 15-year-olds and constructed well-being and need-supportive teaching scales from PISA items. The authors excluded 10 economies that did not include either need-supportive teaching or well-being data (Australia, Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Israel, Lebanon, North Macedonia, Norway, New Zealand, and Singapore), leaving 70 economies. Missing data were handled via MCMC multiple imputation (parent support missing reported as 2.6% as the highest among variables). The analysis then proceeded with measurement-model testing and two-level HLM where student-level covariates (need-supportive teaching, gender, student SES, immigration status, parent support) were level 1 and school SES and school composition were level 2.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-level HLM (standardized β): Need-supportive teaching β = 0.11 (p < .001). ICC = 0.08. Model fit indices reported for measurement model (CFI/TLI/RMSEA) but no predictive ML metrics.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 the study leveraged Need-supportive teaching, Parent support, Student SES (ESCS), Gender, and Immigration status to predict Positive affect, finding that Need-supportive teaching positively predicted Positive affect (β = 0.11, p < .001). This indicates that strengthening need-supportive teaching practices may improve students’ day-to-day emotional well-being, though the cross-sectional design limits causal claims.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-level HLM (standardized β): Need-supportive teaching β = -0.04 (p < .001). ICC = 0.10. Model fit indices reported for measurement model but no predictive ML metrics.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 the study leveraged Need-supportive teaching, Parent support, Gender, Student SES (ESCS), and Immigration status to predict Negative affect, finding that Need-supportive teaching negatively predicted Negative affect (β = -0.04, p < .001). This indicates that adopting autonomy-supportive, competence-supportive, and relatedness-supportive teaching may reduce students’ negative emotions, while cultural differences in negative-emotion interpretation suggest effects may vary by context.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-level HLM (standardized β): Need-supportive teaching β = 0.11 (p < .001). ICC = 0.08. Model fit indices reported for measurement model but no predictive ML metrics.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 the study leveraged Need-supportive teaching, Parent support, Student SES (ESCS), Gender, and Immigration status to predict Life satisfaction, finding that Need-supportive teaching positively predicted Life satisfaction (β = 0.11, p < .001). This indicates that teacher practices that support students’ basic psychological needs may be a practical lever for improving students’ overall satisfaction with life, even after accounting for key demographic and socioeconomic covariates.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) Eudaimonic well-being: Meaning in life
main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-level HLM (standardized β): Need-supportive teaching β = 0.12 (p < .001). ICC = 0.08. Model fit indices reported for measurement model but no predictive ML metrics.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 the study leveraged Need-supportive teaching, Parent support, Student SES (ESCS), Gender, and Immigration status to predict Meaning in life, finding that Need-supportive teaching positively predicted Meaning in life (β = 0.12, p < .001). This indicates that need-supportive teaching may support eudaimonic functioning (purpose/meaning), suggesting that well-being-oriented teacher training could complement academic-focused interventions, though causality cannot be established from cross-sectional associations.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-level HLM (standardized β): Need-supportive teaching β = 0.10 (p < .001). ICC = 0.09. Model fit indices reported for measurement model but no predictive ML metrics.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 the study leveraged Need-supportive teaching, Parent support, Student SES (ESCS), Gender, and Immigration status to predict School belonging, finding that Need-supportive teaching positively predicted School belonging (β = 0.10, p < .001). This indicates that implementing need-supportive instructional approaches may strengthen students’ sense of acceptance and inclusion at school, supporting school climate and retention goals even across diverse cultural groups.

data.outcome_summary: This cross-cultural study used PISA 2018 (OECD) secondary data for 513,295 students across 70 economies to examine whether need-supportive teaching is associated with three subjective well-being components (positive affect, negative affect, life satisfaction) and two additional well-being components (meaning in life and school belonging). The authors estimated two-level HLM models (students nested in schools) after testing a six-factor measurement model and measurement invariance across eight Schwartz (2009) cultural groups. Need-supportive teaching showed small but statistically significant standardized associations with positive affect (β = 0.11), life satisfaction (β = 0.11), meaning in life (β = 0.12), and school belonging (β = 0.10), and a negative association with negative affect (β = −0.04), with ICCs around 0.08–0.10. Missing data were addressed via MCMC multiple imputation. Limitations include cross-sectional design (no causal inference) and reliance on self-reported PISA items; the manuscript excerpt does not report whether PISA sampling weights were applied.
